title: Formation of a new form exterminates its parent and transitional varieties

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Formation of a new form exterminates its parent and transitional varieties

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Because each new form tends in a fully stocked country to supplant and exterminate its less improved parent and other competing forms, the parent and all transitional varieties are generally exterminated by the process that forms the new species.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Hence, if we look at each species as descended from some other unknown form, both the parent and all the transitional varieties will generally have been exterminated by the very process of formation and perfection of the new form.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter VI, “Difficulties on Theory”; section “Absence or rarity of transitional varieties.”. Scope: all species in fully stocked regions

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch06-01: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.57

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Selected fossil series can test temporal replacement, but preservation and ancestry uncertainty are substantial. Existing data rarely distinguish extinction by competitive species formation from coincident turnover.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: In densely sampled lineage series, test whether appearance and improvement of derived forms precede decline and disappearance of inferred parents and intermediates. A repeated temporal replacement pattern supports the prediction; long coexistence or ancestor persistence refutes its generality.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Replacement can be driven by environment rather than new-form competition.

Direct ancestors and transitional varieties are hard to identify.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The process claim requires catching parent and transitional forms in the act of disappearing, which almost no dataset records directly. Fossil ranges and character matrices support a proxy in a few dense clades, and modern abundance series are too short for speciation. Taxonomic practice and missing strata both predict the absence of intermediates, so discrimination is limited.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: During intervals when a new form becomes morphologically distinct, test whether parental and transitional populations disappear rather than persist beside it. Early presence and later absence of intermediates, beyond a preservation null, would support the claim; routine coexistence of parent, transitional, and descendant forms would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Transitional varieties are seldom named as populations in the fossil record.

Incomplete preservation removes intermediates whether or not competition did.

Modern time series rarely span speciation.
